rationale: The book's identification — lamp oil as truth and correction received inwardly and stored as proven obedience — is derived from a network of texts that actually address lamp oil, wisdom/folly, storing, and buying, whereas the common Holy Spirit reading rests almost entirely on anointing texts that the book shows belong to a lexically and legally distinct substance. Exodus 25:6 lists 'oil for the light' and 'spices for anointing oil' as separate provisions, and Exodus 30:22-33 restricts the compounded anointing oil to sanctuary use; the standard Spirit proof texts (1 Sam 16:13; Acts 10:38; Isa 61:1) all concern anointing/appointment, not lamp fuel. The book's positive case is unusually tight for the parable's specific mechanics: Proverbs 6:23 puts commandment=lamp, law=light, and reproofs of instruction in one sentence; Psalm 141:5 (with Prov 27:5-9) names reproof 'an excellent oil'; Proverbs 21:20 stages the exact inventory (oil stored in the dwelling of the wise, exhausted by the fool); Proverbs 23:23 commands the purchase ('buy the truth') that Matthew 25:9 commands ('go... buy'); and Jer 31:33/Ezek 36:27 supply the inward storing while keeping the Spirit as cause rather than referent. Crucially, the book explains the parable's mechanics that the Spirit reading cannot: the oil must be bought (Acts 8:20 anathematizes buying the Spirit), is finite and divisible ('lest there be not enough for us and you' — but the Spirit is given 'not by measure,' John 3:34), must be accumulated beforehand (the Spirit fell on Cornelius in a moment), and cannot be transferred (a neighbor's obedience cannot burn for you, whereas the Spirit is ministered through laying on of hands, Acts 8:17). It also defuses the strongest counter proof text on its own wording: in Zechariah 4 the angel identifies the olive branches as 'the two anointed ones' and never says the oil is the Spirit. No alternative I can formulate accounts for these details with fewer unsupported steps.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Lamp oil symbolizes the Holy Spirit — the indwelling, sustaining presence of the Spirit that genuine believers possess and mere professors lack — grounded in the oil-Spirit association of anointing (1 Sam 16:13; Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38), Zechariah 4's Spirit-word over the oil-fed lampstand, and the tabernacle lamps perpetually burning on pure oil as a type of the Spirit sustaining spiritual life.
counter_case: Zechariah 4:1-6 places 'Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit' as the interpretive word over a lampstand supplied with oil, the closest OT scene joining oil, lamp, and Spirit.
1 Samuel 16:13 links pouring oil directly with the Spirit coming upon David, establishing oil as the standing biblical sign of the Spirit's coming.
Acts 10:38 and Isaiah 61:1/Luke 4:18 make anointing-with-oil language explicitly Spirit language in the NT's own idiom.
Exodus 27:20-21 and Leviticus 24:1-4: the perpetually burning sanctuary lamp fueled by pure oil is a natural type of divine life sustained by the Spirit, not by human effort.
1 John 2:20,27 and 2 Cor 1:21-22: the abiding 'anointing' in believers is effectively identified with the Spirit's indwelling.
On this reading the foolish virgins are professors without the indwelling Spirit (cf. Rom 8:9), which cannot be borrowed from another believer — matching the refusal to share.
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains the parable's purchase command: Prov 23:23 'buy the truth' matches Matt 25:9, while Acts 8:20 makes buying the Spirit a cursed idea — the counter-reading collides with its own canon here.

Explains finiteness and non-transferability: obedience accumulated over a life is genuinely zero-sum in time and unlendable; the Spirit is given 'not by measure' (John 3:34) and can be given instantly (Acts 10:44) or through ministers (Acts 8:17).
Respects the law's own distinction between lamp oil and anointing oil (Ex 25:6; 27:20; 30:22-33), which removes the anointing-Spirit texts as definitions of the virgins' oil.

Completes Proverbs 6:23's own triad: commandment=lamp, law=light, reproof=way of life, with Ps 141:5 and Prov 27:5-9 supplying reproof/counsel as oil — a cross-text chain in the same semantic field as the parable.
Prov 21:20 independently stages wise/fool/oil-stored-vs-spent, the parable's exact three terms, and Prov 31:18 joins purchase and an unquenched night lamp.

Handles Zech 4 on its precise wording (branches = 'the two anointed ones'; the oil is never glossed as the Spirit) and keeps Ezek 36:27's order: Spirit as cause, walking in statutes as the produced store.
Coheres with the parable's stated moral divide (wise doer vs foolish hearer, Matt 7:24-26; 1 John 2:4) and with Matt 5:16 defining the resulting light as visible good works.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The Spirit reading has massive traditional and homiletic attestation and matches the broad biblical oil-Spirit association in anointing contexts.
Zechariah 4 does verbally place the Spirit at the center of an oil-and-lamp vision, and a typological (rather than word-for-word) reading can still take the oil as the Spirit's supply.
Romans 8:9 ('if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his') gives the Spirit reading a clean theological fit with the shut door.
It avoids resting a symbol identification partly on a single oil=reproof verse (Ps 141:5) and on the homiletic 'pressed fruit' motif.
decisive_sources: Exodus 25:6 with Exodus 27:20 and 30:22-33 (lamp oil legally distinct from anointing oil, severing the anointing-Spirit proof texts from the parable)
Proverbs 6:23 with Psalm 141:5 and Proverbs 27:5-9 (lamp/light/reproof triad; reproof named 'excellent oil')
Proverbs 21:20 (oil stored in the dwelling of the wise, spent by the fool — the parable's inventory)
Proverbs 23:23 with Matthew 25:9 and Acts 8:20 (oil must be bought; the Spirit cannot be)
Zechariah 4:6-14 (angel identifies the branches as 'anointed ones,' never the oil as the Spirit)
Ezekiel 36:27 and Jeremiah 31:33 (Spirit as cause producing kept statutes written inwardly)
1 John 2:4 with Psalm 119:11 and Proverbs 7:1-3 (truth/commandments possessed inwardly vs professed outwardly)
unresolved_objections: The identification of oil specifically as reproof/instruction leans heavily on Psalm 141:5, a single explicit verse, supplemented by the thematically looser Proverbs 27:9; the book's own standard asks for patterns across multiple independent witnesses.

Modern critical caution that parable details need not carry one-to-one referents is not refuted, only outweighed; if the oil is merely narrative furniture for readiness, both allegorical readings overreach.

The book's final definition still embeds the Spirit as cause ('fruit of the Spirit stored'), so the practical distance from a sophisticated Spirit reading (Spirit's wrought life vs Spirit Himself) is smaller than the polemic suggests.

The tabernacle lamp-oil typology (perpetual light sustained by pure oil) can still be read pneumatologically without invoking the anointing compound, and the book does not fully close that typological route.
The appeal to Shem Tov's Hebrew Matthew for readings ('bridegroom and bride,' 'lazy fools,' nid'akhu) rests on a late and text-critically contested witness.
